options.text: A rule that most people consider unfair cannot be valid law, because law and morality are one standard in the case at hand.
options.misconception: treats moral disapproval as a test of validity

options.text: A statute is automatically void whenever the judge would have written it differently on the facts given.
options.misconception: confuses legality with a judge's preference

options.text: A long-standing trade custom overrides a clear statute because custom best expresses community values as the record shows.
A rule can be legally binding even when it is morally unattractive, because validity turns on recognized sources rather than private approval in this situation.

questions.explanation: Validity and moral worth are separate inquiries. A rule enacted through a recognized source binds even those who dislike it, and the remedy for a bad rule belongs in the lawmaking process rather than in a judge's private sense of fairness. Here the decisive point is the separation between legal validity and moral approval, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
